old_entry.title: Street Fighter III
old_entry.summary: Street Fighter III: New Generation (Japanese: ストリートファイターIII -New Generation-) is a 1997 fighting game in Capcom's Street Fighter series, originally released as a coin-operated arcade game.
body: Street Fighter III: New Generation (Japanese: ストリートファイターIII -New Generation-) is a 1997 fighting game in Capcom's Street Fighter series, originally released as a coin-operated arcade game. The  sequel to Street Fighter II (1991), it initially discarded every previous character except for Ryu and Ken (hence the New Generation subtitle), introducing an all-new roster led by Alex. Likewise, a new antagonist named Gill took over M. Bison's role from the previous games as the new boss character.

Street Fighter III was produced for the CD-ROM-based CP System III hardware, which allowed for more elaborate 2D graphics than the CPS II-based Street Fighter Alpha games (the previous incarnation of the Street Fighter series), while revamping many of the play mechanics. Despite the popularity of 3D polygonal fighting games at the time, Capcom decided to keep this game in 2D; 3D graphics were instead implemented in the spin-off game, Street Fighter EX.

Street Fighter III was followed by two updates: 2nd Impact in 1997, and 3rd Strike in 1999. A single home version of the game was released for the Dreamcast in 1999 and 2000, in a two-in-one compilation titled Street Fighter III: Double Impact, which consists of New Generation and 2nd Impact. Street Fighter III received a mainly positive reception, but did not manage to be a hit like its predecessor; it was followed by Street Fighter IV (2008).

old_entry.title: Diablo
old_entry.subtitle: The Click That Put Role-Playing in Motion
old_entry.summary: Diablo's date is less tidy than a calendar might suggest: copies began circulating at the end of 1996, while Blizzard issued its in-stores announcement on January 3, 1997.
body: Diablo's date is less tidy than a calendar might suggest: copies began circulating at the end of 1996, while Blizzard issued its in-stores announcement on January 3, 1997. That logistical uncertainty contrasts with the clarity of the game itself. Diablo takes dungeon crawling, makes it immediate through the mouse, builds variable rooms and rewards, and places Battle.net cooperation inside the adventure's normal flow. Within weeks, Tristram becomes the laboratory for a form of action RPG whose basic rhythm would remain recognizable for decades.

The original Diablo proposal describes a game with a very different rhythm. David Brevik and Condor imagined a turn-based RPG built around randomly generated dungeons and the replayability of the roguelikes Brevik loved. Its intended look was also closer to a DOS project with animation initially conceived around claymation. The turning point came when Blizzard pushed for real time. The team did not accept the idea immediately, fearing the loss of turn-based tactical precision. That resistance matters: Diablo did not begin as a simple action game with statistics, but as an attempt to preserve role-playing depth and randomness while completely changing how the player gives commands. Its identity emerged from that tension.

Brevik has described the decisive transformation as a prototype moment: he changed the game so the character could move and attack in real time, then clicked on a skeleton. The action felt immediately more physical than he had expected. The mouse unified movement, targeting, combat and item pickup, reducing the distance between intention and result. Diablo keeps numbers, equipment, levels and RPG decisions, but places them in a flow where every second creates new threats. This apparent simplicity does not remove strategy; it moves it from discrete commands to continuous management of space, speed, health and priorities. This is where the dungeon crawler changes posture: it is no longer only consulted, but almost played like an instrument.

Beneath Tristram, the cathedral is not a map to learn once. Diablo combines rooms, corridors, stairs, treasure, traps and monsters in variable configurations, so a new run can preserve the broad shape of the descent without repeating the exact route. The same principle drives items: rewards after combat are uncertain and can change how a character develops. Randomization and loot reinforce each other. If the player cannot know what waits behind the next door, future equipment cannot be fully planned either. Blizzard therefore creates a structural reason to begin again. Repetition is not only a way to replay the story, but a method for producing a different version of the same journey.

old_entry.title: Tekken 3
old_entry.summary: Tekken 3 (鉄拳3) is a 1997 fighting game developed and published by Namco.
body: Tekken 3 (鉄拳3) is a 1997 fighting game developed and published by Namco. It is the third installment in the Tekken series and the first game built on the Namco System 12 arcade hardware. The game takes place nineteen years after Tekken 2 (1995) and features a largely new cast of characters, including the debut of several staple characters such as Jin Kazama, Ling Xiaoyu and Bryan Fury, and adds a sidestepping ability to every character. Tekken 3 was ported to the PlayStation in 1998 with additional content, including a beat 'em up mode called Tekken Force.

The game was a major hit for both arcades and consoles, selling 35,000 arcade units and 8.36 million PlayStation copies worldwide, making Tekken 3 the fifth best-selling PlayStation game. Since its release, Tekken 3 has been cited as one of the greatest games of all time. It was followed by Tekken Tag Tournament (1999) and its direct sequel, Tekken 4 (2001). Later, Tekken 3's arcade version was included within Tekken 5 on PlayStation 2, while the console port was re-released as part of Sony's PlayStation Classic.

old_entry.title: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night
old_entry.summary: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night is a 1997 action role-playing game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation and Sega Saturn.
body: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night is a 1997 action role-playing game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation and Sega Saturn. It is a direct sequel to Castlevania: Rondo of Blood, set five years after its events. It was directed and produced by Toru Hagihara, with Koji Igarashi acting as assistant director.

It features Dracula's dhampir son Alucard (returning from Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse) as the protagonist, as he explores Dracula's castle (which reemerges following the disappearance of Richter Belmont) and fights to prevent his father from fully regaining his lost power. Its design marks a break from previous entries in the series, re-introducing the exploration, nonlinear level design, and role-playing elements first experimented with in Castlevania II: Simon's Quest.

Symphony of the Night initially sold poorly. However, it gradually gained sales through word-of-mouth and became a sleeper hit, developing a cult following and selling over 700,000 units in the United States and Japan. The game garnered acclaim, often cited by critics as one of the best video games of all time, praising its gameplay innovations, atmosphere, visuals and soundtrack with criticism directed towards the voice acting. It is also considered the definitive pioneer of the Metroidvania genre, combining the two games and inspiring numerous exploration-based action-adventure games ever since. Symphony of the Night would have a lasting impact on the Castlevania series, with numerous subsequent mainline entries adopting its gameplay model.

old_entry.title: GoldenEye 007
old_entry.summary: GoldenEye 007 is a 1997 first-person shooter game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.
body: GoldenEye 007 is a 1997 first-person shooter game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is based on the 1995 James Bond film GoldenEye, with the player controlling the secret agent James Bond to prevent a criminal syndicate from using a satellite weapon. They navigate a series of levels to complete objectives, such as recovering or destroying objects, while shooting enemies. In a multiplayer mode, up to four players compete in several deathmatch scenarios via split-screen.

Development began in January 1995. An inexperienced team led by Martin Hollis developed GoldenEye 007 over two and a half years. The game was conceived as a side-scrolling platform game for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, but evolved into a 3D shooter for the Nintendo 64 inspired by Doom (1993) and Virtua Cop (1994). Rare visited the GoldenEye set for reference, and Eon Productions and Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM) allowed them to expand the game with sequences and characters not featured in the film.

GoldenEye 007 was released in Japan on 23 August 1997, North America on 25 August 1997, and the United Kingdom on 7 November 1997, two years after the release of the film but shortly before the release of its sequel Tomorrow Never Dies. It faced low expectations from the gaming media during development. However, it received critical acclaim and sold over eight million copies, making it the third-best-selling Nintendo 64 game. The game was praised for its visuals, gameplay depth and variety, and multiplayer mode. In 1998, it received the BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Award, as well as four awards from the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences.

GoldenEye 007 demonstrated the viability of home consoles as platforms for first-person shooters and signalled a transition from Doom-like shooters to a more grounded style. It pioneered features such as atmospheric single-player missions, widescreen gaming, stealth elements, and console multiplayer deathmatch. The game is considered to be one of the most influential and greatest video games ever made, with many of its elements, such as the Klobb gun, leaving an enduring impression in video game culture. A spiritual successor, Perfect Dark, was released in 2000, while a remake developed by Eurocom, also titled GoldenEye 007, was released in 2010. The original game was rereleased in January 2023 on Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S via Xbox Game Pass and Nintendo Switch via the Nintendo Classics service.

GoldenEye 007 reached North America on Nintendo 64 on August 25, 1997. It was not the game's first release, which had taken place in Japan on August 23, but it became the date on which many Western players encountered a project that changed the idea of the console shooter. Rare built missions around objectives, alarms, rooms and routes rather than simple corridors to clear. Its famous split-screen multiplayer began almost as an internal experiment and ended up turning living rooms into small social arenas. The film licence did not suffocate the game. It became material to be taken apart and rebuilt around interactive timing, space and rules. GoldenEye showed that adapting a movie means finding a playable equivalent, not merely reproducing scenes.

GoldenEye 007 builds levels where simply reaching the exit is not enough. A mission may require photographing a target, retrieving a key, sabotaging equipment or protecting a character, while higher difficulty can add more objectives. That structure turns spaces into places to understand rather than corridors filled with targets. Guards, cameras and alarms allow cautious play before gunfire begins. For a game born from a film license, its key invention is therefore procedural: Bond is not represented only in cutscenes but through a list of responsibilities that changes how the player moves and reads each room.

GoldenEye 007's multiplayer was built late in development, yet it came to define the game's collective memory. Four people share one television, inevitably see one another's screens and negotiate informal rules about characters, weapons and maps. Split-screen technology reduces the amount of image available to each player, but dramatically expands the social scale of the experience. Every match produces accusations of screen-peeking, temporary alliances and domestic rituals. It is a powerful example of how a relatively compact feature can change the cultural destiny of a project, turning a single-player shooter into a recurring group event.

The game does not follow GoldenEye scene by scene. Rare takes locations, characters and objectives from the film and recomposes them into missions that can support exploration, action and repetition. That freedom matters because a feature film and an interactive level operate on different clocks: something lasting seconds on screen can become an environment studied for half an hour. The choice points toward a more mature model for licensed games, where fidelity does not mean literal copying. GoldenEye remains unmistakably Bond because the player performs the work of an agent, not because every shot of the movie is passively reconstructed.

old_entry.title: SaGa Frontier
old_entry.subtitle: SaGa Frontier Turns Discontinuity into a Form of Freedom
old_entry.summary: On July 11, 1997 Square released SaGa Frontier for PlayStation in Japan.
body: On July 11, 1997 Square released SaGa Frontier for PlayStation in Japan. Seven protagonists open different stories, often set in regions with their own tones and rules. The SaGa series thus brings its idea of nonlinear progression to the new console while adding the linked-technique combo system that Square Enix identifies as one of the game's representative innovations. The result is deliberately irregular: worlds, races and systems can feel autonomous, but that fragmentation is precisely what encourages the player to experiment with very different routes and party builds.

The basic concept of SaGa Frontier is based on its Free Scenario System, in which one can play as any of seven different protagonists, all of whom exist in the same setting, a solar system known as The Regions: a group of planets, each with its own culture, game-level of technology, and form of magic. The game is considered non-linear, in that from the beginning many of the characters are free to go almost anywhere and interact with almost anyone. Travel through most of the Regions is easy due to inter-regional ships traveling regularly between them. The player controls the protagonist on the field screen, a set of interconnecting pre-rendered backgrounds, and is able to speak with a slew of other characters in order to gather information, recruit party members, and initiate quests. Each character has a storyline and a main quest to fulfill, but there are also several optional quests that any of the characters can participate in. Some of the main characters encounter each other during their quests. The storyline of each character also changes depending on who is chosen, what is said in conversation, what events have already occurred, and who is in the adventuring party, a concept first introduced in Romancing SaGa 2.

Players encounter groups of enemies on the field screen, upon which they switch to the battle screen. The battle screen depicts 2D-animated sprites amidst a 3D-rotating background. Battles are turn-based; the player chooses the characters' actions and must allow them, along with those of the enemies, to play out. A variety of weapons, special skills, and magic spells are at the player's disposal. Most skills are learned mid-battle, while many spells are purchased in the game's shops. If certain conditions are met within the battle, party members on either side can create combination attacks for added damage. Winning battles increases player character statistics such as hit points (HP), life points (LP), strength, and quickness. Outside of combat, players can equip and unequip (or "seal") weapons, armor, skills, spells, and items. First introduced in the Game Boy incarnations of the SaGa series, the game contains different races that exist within the Regions: the Humans, the Mystics, the Half-Mystics (half Human and half Mystic), Monsters, and the Mecs (robots).

The player is encouraged to complete each of the seven scenarios one after the other. For added incentive, beating a character's game and saving its completion to the system data adds some bonuses. After beating one character's game, essentially every character in the following game starts off stronger and with better gear than before, and may depend on how many battles players fought in their previous quest that they saved on the system data. Fulfilling all seven main quests allows the player access to the "2nd Division" room, in which the player can fight all final bosses and talk to the game's programmers.

The work's memory then grows from the connection between what is told and what the player is asked to do.

original.old_heading: Combos turn the party into a system of relationships

old_entry.title: Gran Turismo
old_entry.subtitle: The first car does not have to be an impossible dream
old_entry.summary: On December 23, 1997, Gran Turismo was released in Japan on PlayStation after roughly five years of development.
body: On December 23, 1997, Gran Turismo was released in Japan on PlayStation after roughly five years of development. Kazunori Yamauchi wanted to create a realistic driving simulator when the idea was still difficult to sell internally; Motor Toon Grand Prix allowed him to build trust and technology while the project grew in parallel. The initial team consisted of only five people and remained under twenty even toward the end. The game combines vehicle physics, detailed models, engine sounds and a progression structure inspired by role-playing games: racing produces money, money becomes cars or parts, and every modification changes the vehicle's behavior. With more than one hundred models and eleven circuits, Gran Turismo turns the production car into an object to learn, collect and improve, not merely a racing piece.

Yamauchi says that Gran Turismo's physics engine could accept highly detailed parameters, drawn where possible from design data or measurements of real cars. The goal was to make the specific character of each vehicle emerge rather than applying a single response to different models. But precision is not treated as synonymous with difficulty. During testing, the team observed many players entering corners too fast and crashing; Yamauchi therefore decided to make driving more accessible without abandoning the simulation principle. It is a fundamental balance for the series. The physics model has to produce credible behavior, while the game has to help players without real driving experience interpret it. Gran Turismo thus builds a realism oriented toward understanding: it does not ask players to suffer because a car is complex, but to learn why it reacts in a certain way.

Gran Turismo Mode adds a logic of accumulation to racing. Winning produces credits, credits allow the player to buy cars or parts, and modifications can make more demanding events possible. Yamauchi has explicitly connected this structure to his experience with computer role-playing games such as Wizardry and Ultima. The car is therefore not simply selected from a menu before a race: it becomes an investment the player develops over time. Suspension, tires or an increase in power change both performance and the emotional relationship with an already familiar machine. Progression also creates value for modest cars, because the first affordable vehicle is not necessarily an exotic dream but a tool to be developed. Racing thus takes on the form of a career, where driving mastery and resource management advance together.

The official page for the first Gran Turismo recalls more than one hundred models and over one hundred and forty-six variants, a catalogue that includes many cars recognizable from everyday roads rather than only competition prototypes. This choice changes what the player desires. Appeal does not depend solely on driving the fastest car, but on comparing different versions, drivetrains, weights and characters. A car seen in a parking lot or magazine can become an object of virtual study. Gran Turismo thus builds a bridge between video games and car culture, giving gameplay significance to differences that other titles might have treated as simple visual variations. The catalogue matters because it makes simulation readable through comparison: by driving many vehicles, the player learns that power, weight distribution and mechanical setup produce different sensations and begins to recognize them.

Gran Turismo does not seek realism only in tire behavior. Yamauchi recalls how important light was and how impressed the team felt when it saw a car model rotate in real time with convincing reflections on the bodywork. On the first PlayStation, achieving this required careful use of geometry, textures and shading because the amount of detail available was limited. The solution was not to reproduce every surface, but to choose visual signals capable of conveying metal, glass, volume and paint. Replays also use more cinematic camera angles to present the vehicle as an object to observe as well as control. The visual direction therefore supports the simulation project: if one car has to feel different from another when driven, it also has to appear as a material object with sufficiently credible proportions and light.

The perceived scale of Gran Turismo contrasts with the size of its original team. Yamauchi and Shuhei Yoshida recall a group of five people at the beginning and fewer than twenty even toward the end of a development process lasting about five years. Each member therefore takes on broad responsibility and the project advances slowly, while physics, graphics, automotive data and content all have to grow together. Yamauchi had already begun working on the idea while making Motor Toon Grand Prix, using that more easily approved title to build experience and internal trust. The birth of Gran Turismo is therefore also a story of organization: not a huge production launched with unlimited resources, but a project sustained for years by a small, specialized group. Its later success would allow Yamauchi to formalize Polyphony Digital as an independent studio.

Yamauchi remembers the Japanese launch day, December 23, 1997, as an almost unreal moment. He visited major stores and saw people lining up to buy a game the team had kept close for years. The series' official page confirms that date and presents the first entry as the origin of the Real Driving Simulator. The transition from production to audience is especially significant for such a long project: until the previous day, every problem belongs to a small group, then suddenly millions of interpretations of driving, cars and difficulty begin to exist outside the studio. Success does not end the work, because it becomes the foundation for a much broader sequel and a growing relationship with the automotive industry. That launch turns an experiment in simulation into a serial language destined to evolve alongside PlayStation.

story_headings: The first car does not have to be an impossible dream
Simulation begins with parameters, but must remain drivable
A racing game borrows progression from RPGs
Production cars become protagonists
Light on the bodywork becomes part of credibility
Five people begin a project that will take five years
On December 23, the project stops belonging only to the team
